I am sitting under tall trees, with a great wind boiling like surf about the tops of them, so that their living load of leaves rocks and roars in something that is at once exultation and agony. I feel, in fact, as if I were actually sitting at the bottom of the sea among mere anchors and ropes, while over my head and over the green twilight of water sounded the everlasting rush of waves and the toil and crash and shipwreck of tremendous ships. The wind tugs at the trees as if it might pluck them root and all out of the earth like tufts of grass. Or, to try yet another desperate figure of speech for this unspeakable energy, the trees are straining and tearing and lashing as if they were a tribe of dragons each tied by the tail.

As I look at these top-heavy giants tortured by an invisible and violent witchcraft, a phrase comes back into my mind. I remember a little boy of my acquaintance who was once walking in Battersea Park under just such torn skies and tossing trees. He did not like the wind at all; it blew in his face too much; it made him shut his eyes; and it blew off his hat, of which he was very proud. He was, as far as I remember, about four. After complaining repeatedly of the atmospheric unrest, he said at last to his mother, “Well, why don’t you take away the trees, and then it wouldn’t wind.”

Nothing could be more intelligent or natural than this mistake. Any one looking for the first time at the trees might fancy that they were indeed vast and titanic fans, which by their mere waving agitated the air around them for miles. Nothing, I say, could be more human and excusable than the belief that it is the trees which make the wind. Indeed, the belief is so human and excusable that it is, as a matter of fact, the belief of about ninety-nine out of a hundred of the philosophers, reformers, sociologists, and politicians of the great age in which we live. My small friend was, in fact, very like the principal modern thinkers; only much nicer.

.....

In the little apologue or parable which he has thus the honour of inventing, the trees stand for all visible things and the wind for the invisible. The wind is the spirit which bloweth where it listeth; the trees are the material things of the world which are blown where the spirit lists. The wind is philosophy, religion, revolution; the trees are cities and civilisations. We only know that there is a wind because the trees on some distant hill suddenly go mad. We only know that there is a real revolution because all the chimney-pots go mad on the whole skyline of the city.

message.content:
Here I find myself beneath towering trees, where a fierce wind roars like ocean waves crashing against the shore, causing the branches and leaves to sway and create a symphony of both joy and distress. It feels as though I am submerged at the ocean’s floor, surrounded by anchors and ropes, while above me the relentless sound of waves echoes, accompanied by the labor and wreckage of colossal ships. The wind pulls at the trees with such force that it seems capable of uprooting them, as if they were mere tufts of grass. Alternatively, to depict this indescribable force in another manner, one might imagine the trees straining and thrashing as if they were a band of dragons, each tethered by its tail.

As I observe these towering giants, tormented by an unseen yet violent energy, a memory surfaces. I recall a young boy I once knew who was strolling through Battersea Park beneath similarly turbulent skies and swaying trees. He was not fond of the wind; it blew directly into his face, causing him to squint and even blowing off his cherished hat. If my recollection serves me right, he was around four years old. After expressing his dissatisfaction with the windy conditions multiple times, he finally turned to his mother and inquired, “Well, why don’t you take away the trees, and then it wouldn’t wind?”

This misinterpretation could not be more logical or relatable. To someone witnessing the trees for the first time, it would be easy to assume they were gigantic fans, stirring the air around them for miles simply through their movement. In fact, nothing could be more understandable than the notion that the trees are responsible for creating the wind. This perspective is so inherently human that it represents the belief held by nearly ninety-nine percent of the philosophers, reformers, sociologists, and politicians of our contemporary era. My young friend, in his innocent reasoning, mirrored the thoughts of many modern thinkers, albeit with a much sweeter disposition.

In the little story or parable that he unwittingly crafted, the trees symbolize all that is visible, while the wind represents the invisible forces at play. The wind embodies the spirit that moves freely; the trees represent the tangible aspects of our world that are influenced by that spirit. The wind signifies philosophy, religion, and revolution, while the trees stand for cities and civilizations. We recognize the existence of the wind only when the trees on a distant hill begin to sway wildly. Similarly, we become aware of a genuine revolution when we see the chimney pots on the city skyline behaving erratically.
